en: The Theravāda Vinaya:
Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga,
Pārājika Section
6. The Training Rule on Concealing a Fault At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the bhikkhunī Sundarīnandā was pregnant by Sāḷha, the grandson of Migāra.
She concealed [the pregnancy] as long as the fetus was immature;
when the fetus had matured, she left the community and gave birth.
The bhikkhunīs said this to the bhikkhunī Thullanandā:
“Lady, Sundarīnandā has recently gone forth and given birth.
Could it be that she was already pregnant while still being a bhikkhunī?
“Yes, lady,” she replied.
“But why, noble lady, knowing that a bhikkhunī has committed an offense entailing defeat, do you neither reprove her yourself nor report it to the Saṅgha?
“Whatever disrepute she has is my own disrepute; whatever ill-fame she has is my own ill-fame; whatever infamy she has is my own infamy; whatever loss she suffers is my own loss.
Noble lady, why should I report my own disrepute, my own ill-fame, my own infamy, and my own loss to others?”
Those bhikkhunīs who were modest … [as before] … complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
“How can the noble lady Thullanandā, knowing that a bhikkhunī has committed an offense entailing defeat, neither reprove her herself nor report it to the Saṅgha?
Then those bhikkhunīs reported this matter to the bhikkhus.
The bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then, on that occasion and in that connection, the Blessed One had the community of bhikkhus assembled and questioned the bhikkhus:
“Is it true, bhikkhus, that the bhikkhunī Thullanandā, knowing that another bhikkhunī has committed an offense entailing defeat, neither reproves her herself nor informs the community?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can this be, monks? How indeed can the bhikkhunī Thullanandā, knowing that a bhikkhunī has committed an offense entailing expulsion, neither reprove her herself nor inform the Saṅgha?”
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And furthermore, monks, the nuns should recite this training rule:
‘Whatever nun, knowing that another nun has committed an offense entailing defeat, neither herself admonish her nor encourage others to do so—’”
If she does not inform the community, and when that nun has either died, been expelled, been sent away, or has left the order,
she later says: “Venerable ladies, I already knew that this bhikkhunī was such and such a sister,
yet I did not confront her myself nor inform the community,” she too is defeated.
"She is one who is not to be lived with, a concealer of faults.
As for "whichever," it refers to whichever such person... [and so forth].
"A bhikkhunī" ...
[as before] ... this is the kind of bhikkhunī intended in this context.
"Knows" means:
"She knows it herself," or "others inform her of it," or "she informs him herself.
"One who has committed an offense entailing defeat" means one who has committed any one of the eight offenses entailing defeat.
"He should not rebuke himself" means he should not rebuke himself.
"He should not inform the community" means...
She should not inform other bhikkhunīs.
And when she is "standing" or "deceased":
one who is standing is said to be standing in her own [monastic] marks.
"Cutā" means one who has passed away.
"Nāsitā" means one who has either left of her own accord or has been expelled by others.
"Dismissed" means she is said to have gone over to another sectarian order.
Later, she might say: "Venerable ladies, even before, I knew that this bhikkhunī was such and such a sister. Yet they do not themselves accuse her.
Either I myself will not reprove her,
nor will I inform the Saṅgha,
nor will I inform other bhikkhunīs.
This too is said with reference to the previous [cases].
"She becomes one who has committed a pārājika offense" means:
Just as a withered leaf, once released from its stalk, is incapable of becoming green again, even so, a bhikkhunī who thinks,

"Knowing that a bhikkhunī has committed an offense involving defeat, I will neither reprove her myself nor report it to the community," becomes at the mere moment of relinquishing that burden a non-Samaṇī, a non-daughter of the Sakyans. Therefore, she is said to be one who has committed an offense involving defeat.
"Non-residence":
residence means performing formal acts together, reciting the scriptures together, and training under the same rules. This is what is called "residence.
That [residence] does not exist with her; therefore it is called "non-residence."
There is no offense if one does not report it thinking, "There will be strife, quarreling, contention, or dispute in the Saṅgha," or if one does not report it thinking,
"There will be a schism in the Saṅgha or a fracture in the Saṅgha."
If she does not report it thinking, “This harsh and cruel woman will cause an obstacle to my life or an obstacle to my holy life”;
or if she does not report it because she does not see other suitable bhikkhunīs;
or if she does not report it because she does not wish to conceal it.
If she does not report it, thinking, "It will be known by her own actions," [there is no offense] for one who is insane ... [and so on] ...
for a first-time offender.
The second Pārājika is finished.
